description: Gente dinámica y con ganas de ver ideas y meterle mucho
summary:
Dry spells and unpredictable rainfall are increasingly common worldwide, and knowledge passed down through generations may no longer be enough to secure a good harvest. In Uruguay, the 2022–23 drought caused US$1.9 billion in direct agricultural losses, about 3% of GDP. We built Seasons Ahead to help the people who plan a farm's production choose crop rotations that protect the soil and hold up in a changing climate.

The producer answers a short interview about each field: its soil analysis, priorities, and constraints. Seasons Ahead combines those answers with NASA data on rainfall, climate, soil moisture, vegetation, and terrain, plus national soil maps. For each field, it compares at least three rotations, including the current one, and explains the rationale, evidence, benefits, gaps, and risks of each. It then recommends one, taking into account the climate that 30 NASA models project for 2026–2035. It also shows how that plan would have performed in every season since 2000 on the producer's own land. A report for their agronomist and an SI assistant help them discuss the options, but the final decision stays with them.
details:
What it does

Seasons Ahead is a web app that helps the person who plans a farm's production choose a crop rotation for each part of a field. It works as a conversation. The producer locates the field on a map (by adress, by drawing it, by uploading a file or by typing coordinates), splits it into sections if they are managed differently, and answers a short interview: what is grown today, the soil analysis, livestock, machinery, land tenure, and their primary concerns about soil, water, climate risk, income, forage, simplicity and diversification.

How it works

For each section, the app gathers the data on its own:

  • Rainfall: daily satellite rainfall from GPM IMERG since 2000. NASA POWER gives temperature, radiation, humidity and wind since 1991, and rainfall before 2000 (adjusted to match IMERG). In Uruguay, POWER temperatures are corrected month by month with seven national weather stations.
  • Terrain: SRTM elevation at 30 m, to measure slope and slope length square by square.
  • Vegetation: MODIS NDVI (250 m, since 2000) and Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (30 m), to see what grew each season and when the soil was left bare.
  • Soil moisture: SMAP L4 root-zone moisture and GLDAS, to check the app's own water balance against independent NASA estimates, including past droughts.
  • Future climate: NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, the average and range of 30 climate models for 2026-2035 under a medium-emissions scenario.
  • Soil: Uruguay's national soil maps; ISRIC SoilGrids anywhere else; USDA SSURGO soils and the Cropland Data Layer (each field's past crops) in the United States.
  • The producer's own lab analysis and personal experience takes priority.

Then the engine:

  1. Runs a daily water balance for each crop (FAO-56 method) and counts how many years out of ten each crop would suffer drought, frost or heat during its critical stage. It uses 35 real years of weather, shifted to the climate projected for 2026-2035.
  2. Estimates soil loss with the Universal Soil Loss Equation and checks it against what the soil can tolerate. 4,000 simulations give a range and the chance of going over that limit.
  3. Scores the current rotation and the candidate rotations on seven criteria, weighted by the producer's priorities. Rotations that keep erosion within tolerance come first. Because priorities say which criteria matter more, not exact weights, the app tries 2,000 sets of weights that respect that order and shows how often the recommended rotation still comes out on top.
  4. For at least three rotations, including the current one, it explains the rationale, the evidence, the benefits, the gaps and the risks, and adds the FAO/IIASA crop suitability as a second opinion.
  5. Replays the recommended plan in every season since 2000 on that same land, next to what was actually grown.

The result is a map of the field colored by crop, season by season, with a 3D terrain view, a calendar, and a printable report for the agronomist. An AI assistant answers questions about the plan, but every number comes from the engine, not from the chat. Without an AI key, the app runs a guided version with the same analysis.

Benefits and intended impact

Public NASA data becomes an answer about one specific field, in terms a producer already uses: "3 years out of 10, the soybean flowers in a drought." Each figure shows where it comes from and what we still don't know about it, so the agronomist can check it. We started in Uruguay, where Soil Use Plans are mandatory and the 2022-23 drought cost about 3% of GDP, but the global datasets let it work anywhere: the example fields are in Uruguay, Chile and Germany, and it also handles fields in the United States. The decision always stays with the producer.

Tools

Backend in Python (FastAPI, NumPy, pandas, Shapely). Frontend in TypeScript with React, Vite, Leaflet, three.js and Turf. Google Earth Engine and NASA's Earthdata services (Giovanni, AppEEARS, ORNL DAAC, CMR, GIBS) for the data. Hosted on Vercel. The chat assistant uses Google's Gemini API. Much of the code was written with the help of Claude Code (Anthropic) and Gemini (Google); the team designed the method, checked the data and reviewed the results.

What makes it creative

It asks instead of making the producer fill in forms. It tests the recommendation against 25 real seasons on the producer's own land, not just against averages. It shows the plan on the field's real terrain in 3D. It is honest about uncertainty: ranges, how firm a recommendation is, and the data that is missing.

What we considered

Datasets come at very different scales (about 50 km for POWER, 30 m for Landsat and Sentinel-2), so everything is brought down to each section of the field. We compared sources and fixed what we found: POWER shows almost no rain in central Uruguay from October 2022 to July 2023 and overstates summer heat, so we used IMERG for rainfall and national stations for temperature. Clouds hide many satellite passes, so the app works with the clear dates only. Many producers are not used to technology, so the language is plain and the producer's own data always wins over the satellite.
dataRefs: GPM IMERG V07 daily rainfall (Final and Late Run)
NASA Giovanni (GES DISC), time series of IMERG
SMAP L4 Global Root Zone Soil Moisture (SPL4SMGP v008)
ECOSTRESS L2T LSTE V2 land surface temperature, 70 m
NASA GIBS map layers (Blue Marble, HLS)
projectRefs: USDA-NRCS SSURGO via Soil Data Access (US soils)
USDA-NASS Cropland Data Layer and crop statistics (US past crops, 2012 drought yields)
FAO/IIASA GAEZ v4 crop suitability (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)
MGAP-DGRN Uruguay: CONEAT soils, erodibility, soil-loss tolerance, R factor, cadastre
Erosión 6.0 USLE/RUSLE tables (MGAP / Facultad de Agronomía, UdelaR)
Agrociencia Uruguay v23 n2 (canola soil-loss ratios)
DIEA/MGAP Anuario Estadístico Agropecuario (Uruguay crop yields)
INIA Uruguay, Revista INIA no. 83 (soybean price outlook)
INUMET weather station temperatures (Uruguay open data)
AWS Terrain Tiles (Tilezen), SRTM elevation tiles
IDE Uruguay address and place search
OpenStreetMap: map tiles, Nominatim search, Overpass roads (ODbL)
Esri World Imagery basemap (used with attribution)
Google Gemini API (the app's chat assistant, SI)
Claude Code by Anthropic (SI coding assistant)
Leaflet, Leaflet-Geoman and Turf.js (maps and geometry)
Other open-source libraries (Zustand, JSZip, shpjs, togeojson, thinking-orbs, httpx, Pillow, openpyxl, pypdf), listed in the repository
